title: ICE Detains Over 50 Military Spouses and Parents as Immigration Crackdown Hits Armed Forces Families
excerpt: The Trump administration rescinded policies shielding military families from deportation, sparking a Congressional investigation and warnings about military readiness.
body:
• More than 50 spouses and parents of active-duty service members and veterans have been detained by ICE since the Trump administration rescinded military family protections.
  • In April, DHS replaced a policy treating military service as a "significant mitigating factor" with one stating military service "alone does not automatically exempt aliens" from immigration law.
  • Sixty-one members of Congress launched an investigation into the detentions, warning they threaten national security and military recruitment.
  • Cases include an Army staff sergeant's newlywed wife detained at a Louisiana military base and a Marines' father beaten by ICE agents at a California landscaping job.

Staff Sgt. Matthew Blank brought his wife, Annie Ramos, to Fort Polk in Louisiana last month so she could begin the process of receiving military benefits and apply for a green card. The couple had married in March. Days later, federal immigration agents detained Ramos inside the base.

"I never imagined that trying to do the right thing would lead to her being taken away from me," Blank, 23, said in a statement to the Associated Press. "What was supposed to be the happiest week of our lives has turned into one of the hardest."

"If military families are not stable, national security is not stable."

— Lydiah Owiti-Otienoh, Foreign-Born Military Spouse Network

A Policy Reversal

Ramos's case is one of more than 50 documented detentions of military family members since the Trump administration systematically dismantled protections that had been in place for nearly two decades. The policy shift unfolded in stages.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=FiCdbT3ergk

In February 2025, DHS announced it would "no longer exempt classes or categories" of migrants from potential deportation, including military family members and veterans. In April, the administration rescinded a longstanding policy that treated military service as a "significant mitigating factor" in enforcement decisions, replacing it with guidance stating that "military service alone does not automatically exempt aliens from the consequences of violating U.S. immigration laws."

Marine Corps recruiters were subsequently told to stop promoting the military parole-in-place program — a benefit created in 2007 during the Iraq and Afghanistan wars that allowed spouses, parents, and children of service members to stay in the U.S. while pursuing legal status.

Cases Pile Up

The detentions have cut across branches and geographies. In June, a father of two active-duty Marines and one Marine veteran was beaten by ICE agents while working a landscaping job outside an IHOP in California. That same month, the wife of a Marine veteran was detained during a green card application appointment — the very process she was following to legalize her status.

Senator Mark Kelly said he met with the mother of an active-duty Marine who was detained by ICE while caring for her two-year-old grandson at Marine Corps Air Station Yuma. Earlier in the year, a Coast Guardsman's wife was detained and a soldier's wife was deported.

Margaret Stock, a military immigration law expert and retired Army lieutenant colonel, said the irony is unmistakable. "The military continues to hold out the promise of immigration benefits for recruiting purposes, and it's a false promise right now," Stock said. "The recruiters are telling people, 'If you join the military, you're going to be able to get your spouse legal.' And they're not being honest with the recruits."

Congressional Response

In September 2025, 61 Democrats from the Senate and House — led by Senators Elizabeth Warren and Tammy Duckworth and Representatives Chrissy Houlahan and Maggie Goodlander — launched a formal investigation. Their letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and DHS Secretary Kristi Noem demanded answers on how many service members, veterans, and family members had been detained or referred for deportation.

"The Trump administration is blatantly disrespecting our troops and putting our national security at risk," Warren said. "Congressional Democrats are going to use every tool possible to hold the administration accountable."

As of 2024, more than 40,000 noncitizens were serving in the U.S. military, while another 115,000 noncitizen veterans lived in the United States. Veterans' advocate Shawn VanDiver said the situation has become a flashpoint between veterans' organizations and the administration.

"There used to be prior ICE guidance that treated military service as a significant mitigating factor. That doesn't mean anything anymore."

— Shawn VanDiver, U.S. Navy Veteran and Advocate

Impact on Readiness and Recruitment

Military family advocates warn the crackdown could have consequences far beyond individual cases. Research has found that family well-being directly impacts service members' performance during deployment, and USCIS itself has acknowledged that "military preparedness can potentially be adversely affected" when troops worry about their families' immigration status.

DHS has maintained its position. "U.S. military service alone does not automatically grant lawful immigration status, or exempt aliens from the consequences of violating U.S. immigration laws," a DHS spokesperson said.

For Staff Sgt. Blank, whose wife remained in a detention center, the policy debate is personal. "I want my wife home," he said. "And I will not stop fighting until she is back where she belongs, by my side."
nri_angle: Indian-origin service members and their families are among those affected by the policy changes; the crackdown raises questions for all immigrant military families navigating U.S. residency paths.
author: Diaspora Desk
